case_info.caption: A, Transaxial positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) image showing intense bilateral symmetric tonsillar hypermetabolism and bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy hypermetabolism. B, Low-powered (original magnification ×40) and high-powered (inset; original magnification ×400) hematoxylin-eosin stain after tonsillectomy showing lymphoid follicular hyperplasia with a polymorphic inflammatory infiltrate.
case_info.explanation: Almost 1 year after initial presentation, a pathology review of the tonsils found strong positive immunostaining of antitreponemal antibody (Figure 2) associated with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) blood titer of 1:4. Treponemal antibody test (chemiluminescent immunoassay) confirmed the syphilis diagnosis. The patient received intramuscular injections of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin G once a week for 3 weeks, with rapid and complete regression of his symptoms. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection with increased incidence in high-income countries over the past several decades,1with the majority of cases found in men who have sex with men. Acquired syphilis is divided into early syphilis (primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis [ie, acquired within 1 year]) and late syphilis (late latent and tertiary syphilis [ie, acquired after 1 or more years or unknown duration]). Primary syphilis typically begins with a painless ulcer at the site of infection, which can be overlooked when located in the oropharynx, vagina, or rectum. Consequently, many individuals consult clinicians during the secondary stage, which can have various presentations, the most common being a generalized, nonitchy, erythematous maculopapular rash affecting the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Herein, retrospective analysis of the cutaneous eruption 1 year before otolaryngologist referral could suggest secondary syphilis, although RPR and treponemal antibody tests were not performed at that time. Secondary syphilis comprises other symptoms, such as lymphadenopathy, fever, and asthenia. After untreated infection, tertiary syphilis can develop, leading to severe neurological and cardiac complications. Syphilis of the tonsils rarely presents as a symptom of secondary syphilis. At this stage, the condition presents as bilateral tonsillitis rather than unilateral tonsillitis, as in primary syphilis.2Although tonsils usually exhibit redness, swelling, and a gray exudate, often with a diffuse pharyngitis, initial clinical examination can be normal, and tonsillitis is only revealed by positron emission tomography/CT.3,4It is predominantly associated with cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is often delayed and performed using a histopathological analysis (tonsil or lymph node) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption. Confirmation with treponemal antibody test is required because of high false positivity rate of RPR, up to 15%, and treponemal immunohistochemical stain is not specific ofTreponema pallidumand can cross-react with commensal spirochetes of the gastrointestinal tract. Because syphilis cases are increased among men who have sex with men, thorough sexual history might also orientate laboratory workup.5 Regarding differential diagnoses, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is a benign evolving necrotizing histiocytic lymphadenitis mainly described in Asia. It occurs in young women in the context of an infectious or autoimmune condition. It typically presents with painful persistent cervical lymphadenopathy associated with fever and leukopenia.6Excisional biopsy of a lymph node is essential for the diagnosis, showing paracortical areas of fibrinoid necrosis, abundant karyorrhexis, and mononuclear cell infiltration.7 Tonsils are a frequent site of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the Waldeyer ring.8It is a rare subtype of extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma occurring predominantly in older men and presenting as odynophagia with cervical lymphadenopathy. Histopathological analysis shows proliferation of large-sized tumor cells with pleomorphic nuclei and immunohistochemistry stains positive for B-cell antigens with a high Ki67 proliferation index.9 Primary tonsillar tuberculosis represents a rare presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Patients present with recurrent or chronic tonsillitis associated with cervical lymphadenopathy and coexisting pulmonary disease. Diagnosis is based on histopathological examination of the tonsil showing epithelioid granulomas and areas of caseous necrosis. Coloration of Ziehl-Neelsen is frequently positive in this location, showing acid-fast bacilli.10 Syphilis has diverse presentations and is referred to as the “great masquerader.” Given this and the increasing incidence of syphilis, a nontreponemal blood test could be included in the diagnosis approach when facing persistent sore throat and lymphadenopathy.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
